title: 04 — Design a Rate Limiter
html:
04 — Design a Rate Limiter

The one idea: a rate limiter is a counter with a time window, shared by every server that needs to agree on it. The algorithm decides how bursty traffic may be; the shared store (usually Redis) decides whether the limit is correct across instances; the failure policy (open vs closed) decides what happens when that store is down.

Step 1 — Scope

Why rate limit: stop abuse and DoS, cap cost (paid third-party APIs), protect downstream services from overload, enforce plan tiers.

Clarify:

  • Client-side or server-side? → server-side (clients can't be trusted).
  • Throttle by what? → user ID, API key, IP, tenant, endpoint — often several rules.
  • Scale? → distributed across many API instances.
  • Separate service or in-process middleware?
  • Tell the user they're throttled? → yes: HTTP 429 with headers.

Non-functional: accurate, very low added latency (< 1–2 ms), low memory, fault tolerant — the limiter must never take the API down.

Step 2 — High-level design

Where it lives

Option Pros Cons
Client Saves a round trip Trivially bypassed
API gateway Central, no app code, one place for rules Less context (can't limit on business fields easily)
Middleware in each service Full context Every service must implement it consistently
Dedicated limiter service Shared logic, many consumers Extra network hop

Rule of thumb: coarse limits (per IP, per key) at the gateway; business limits (e.g. "5 password resets/hour") in the service.

---
title: Rate limiter — high-level architecture
---
flowchart LR
    C["Client"] --> LB["Load balancer"]
    LB --> M["Rate-limit middleware"]
    M -->|INCR / Lua script| R[("Redis<br/>counters")]
    M -->|allowed| API["API servers"]
    M -->|rejected| X["429 Too Many Requests"]
    Rules[("Rules config<br/>cached locally")] --> M

Response headers

  • X-RateLimit-Limit / X-RateLimit-Remaining / X-RateLimit-Reset (or the IETF RateLimit headers)
  • Retry-After on a 429

Step 3 — Deep dive

3.1 Algorithms

Algorithm How it works Pros Cons
Token bucket Bucket of size b refills at r tokens/s; a request takes a token Allows short bursts, memory-cheap, widely used Two parameters to tune
Leaking bucket Requests enter a FIFO queue processed at a fixed rate Smooth, stable outflow Bursts fill the queue with old requests; newer ones dropped
Fixed window counter Count per clock window (e.g. per minute) Simplest, one counter Burst at window edges can hit 2× the limit
Sliding window log Store a timestamp per request; count those inside the window Exact Memory-heavy: one entry per request
Sliding window counter Current window count + previous window count × overlap % Smooth, cheap, good approximation Approximate (assumes even spread in previous window)

Default choice: token bucket (per key) — it's what most cloud providers use, it tolerates legitimate bursts, and it needs two numbers per key.

Sliding window counter formula:

requests ≈ current_window_count + previous_window_count × (1 − elapsed_fraction_of_current_window)

3.2 Making it correct across servers

Race condition: two instances both read count = 9, both allow, both write 10 → the limit is exceeded.

Fixes:

  • Atomic ops: INCR + EXPIRE for fixed windows.
  • Lua script in Redis for token bucket / sliding window — the whole read-compute-write runs atomically on the Redis server.
  • Avoid distributed locks — too slow for the hot path.

Synchronisation: use one shared store (Redis cluster), not per-instance counters with sticky sessions.

3.3 Rules

- domain: auth
  key: user_id
  descriptor: password_reset
  rate_limit: { unit: hour, requests_per_unit: 5 }
- domain: api
  key: api_key
  rate_limit: { unit: second, requests_per_unit: 100 }

Stored on disk / in config, loaded into memory by workers, refreshed on change.

3.4 Failure policy

Redis unavailable → When to choose
Fail open (allow everything) Limiter protects cost/fairness; availability matters more
Fail closed (reject) Limiter protects security (login brute force) or a fragile dependency
Fall back to local in-memory limits Good compromise: approximate limits per instance

3.5 Performance

  • Keep the check to one Redis round trip (Lua script).
  • Deploy Redis close to the API (same region); multi-region → local limits per region, accept some over-allowance.
  • Hard vs soft limits: soft limits allow brief excess and alert rather than reject.

Step 4 — Wrap-up

  • Limiting at other layers: IP-level in the WAF/firewall (L3/L4), per-connection in the load balancer.
  • Clients should avoid being limited: cache, exponential backoff with jitter, honour Retry-After.
  • Monitor: rejected-request rate per rule. A spike means either an attack or a rule that's too tight.

.NET / Azure mapping

  • ASP.NET Core has built-in rate limiting (Microsoft.AspNetCore.RateLimiting, .NET 7+): AddRateLimiter with FixedWindow, SlidingWindow, TokenBucket and Concurrency limiters, partitioned per key:
builder.Services.AddRateLimiter(o =>
{
    o.RejectionStatusCode = StatusCodes.Status429TooManyRequests;
    o.AddPolicy("per-user", ctx => RateLimitPartition.GetTokenBucketLimiter(
        ctx.User.Identity?.Name ?? ctx.Connection.RemoteIpAddress?.ToString() ?? "anon",
        _ => new TokenBucketRateLimiterOptions
        {
            TokenLimit = 20, TokensPerPeriod = 10,
            ReplenishmentPeriod = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1), QueueLimit = 0
        }));
});
app.UseRateLimiter();
app.MapGet("/orders", GetOrders).RequireRateLimiting("per-user");

⚠️ The built-in limiters are in-process: each instance counts separately. For a global limit across instances, back it with Redis (Lua script via StackExchange.Redis) or enforce it at the gateway.

  • Azure API Management: rate-limit-by-key and quota-by-key policies.
  • Azure Front Door WAF: rate-limit rules per IP at the edge.
  • Polly / Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience: the client side — retries with backoff, circuit breaker when you are the one being limited.

Review checklist

  • Server-side; where it sits and why.
  • Algorithm chosen with its burst behaviour explained.
  • Shared counter store + atomicity (Lua / INCR).
  • 429 + Retry-After + rate-limit headers.
  • Fail-open vs fail-closed decided per use case.
  • Monitoring of rejections.
